entries.a366ccf390ca01390bc3534857dc3822c430c183: <div sID="gen31829" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Eph.3" sID="Eph.3"/> <div eID="gen31829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31830" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31831" type="x-p"/> This chapter consists of two parts. I. Of the account which Paul gives the Ephesians concerning himself, as he was appointed by God to be the apostle of the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.1-Eph.3.13">ver. 1-13</reference>. II. Of his devout and affectionate prayer to God for the Ephesians, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.14-Eph.3.21">ver. 14-21</reference>. We may observe it to have been very much the practice of this apostle to intermix, with his instructions and counsels, intercessions and prayers to God for those to whom he wrote, as knowing that all his instructions and teachings would be useless and vain, except God did co-operate with them, and render them effectual. This is an example that all the ministers of Christ should copy after, praying earnestly that the efficacious operations of the divine Spirit may attend their ministrations, and crown them with success.
entries.a5e3de09f4419b4c30121cae0080c06d4bae694e: <div eID="gen31831" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31830" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Sufferings; Paul's Appointment as an Apostle; Paul's Labours as an Apostle. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 61.)</title> <div sID="gen31832" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> For this cause I Paul, the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles, <hi type="super">2</hi> If ye have heard of the dispensation of the grace of God which is given me to you-ward: 3 How that by revelation he made known unto me the mystery; (as I wrote afore in few words, <hi type="super">4</hi> Whereby, when ye read, ye may understand my knowledge in the mystery of Christ) <hi type="super">5</hi> Which in other ages was not made known unto the sons of men, as it is now revealed unto his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit; 6 That the Gentiles should be fellowheirs, and of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ by the gospel: <hi type="super">7</hi> Whereof I was made a minister, according to the gift of the grace of God given unto me by the effectual working of his power. <hi type="super">8</hi> Unto me, who am less than the least of all saints, is this grace given, that I should preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ; <hi type="super">9</hi> And to make all <hi type="italic">men</hi> see what <hi type="italic">is</hi> the fellowship of the mystery, which from the beginning of the world hath been hid in God, who created all things by Jesus Christ: <hi type="super">10</hi> To the intent that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly <hi type="italic">places</hi> might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God, <hi type="super">11</hi> According to the eternal purpose which he purposed in Christ Jesus our Lord: <hi type="super">12</hi> In whom we have boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him. <hi type="super">13</hi> Wherefore I desire that ye faint not at my tribulations for you, which is your glory. <div eID="gen31832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31833" type="x-p"/> Here we have the account which Paul gives the Ephesians concerning himself, as he was appointed by God the apostle of the Gentiles. <div eID="gen31833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31834" type="x-p"/> I. We may observe that he acquaints them with the tribulations and sufferings which he endured in the discharge of that office, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.1">v. 1</reference>. The first clause refers to the preceding chapter, and may be understood either of these two ways:—1. "<hi type="italic">For this cause,</hi>—for having preached the doctrine contained in the foregoing chapter, and for asserting that the great privileges of the gospel belong not only to the Jews, but to believing Gentiles also, though they are not circumcised,—for this I am now a prisoner, but a <hi type="italic">prisoner of Jesus Christ,</hi> as I suffer in his cause and for his sake, and continue his faithful servant and the object of his special protection and care, while I am thus suffering for him." Observe, Christ's servants, if they come to be prisoners, are his prisoners; and he despises not his prisoners. He thinks never the worse of them for the bad character which the world gives them or the evil treatment that they met with in it. Paul adhered to Christ, and Christ owned him, when he was in prison.—<hi type="italic">For you, Gentiles;</hi> the Jews persecuted and imprisoned him because he was the apostle of the Gentiles, and preached the gospel to them. We may learn hence that the faithful ministers of Christ are to dispense his sacred truths, however disagreeable they may be to some, and whatever they themselves may suffer for doing so. Or, 2. The words may be thus understood:—"<hi type="italic">For this cause,</hi>—since <hi type="italic">you are no more strangers and foreigners</hi> (as <reference osisRef="Eph.2.19">ch. ii. 19</reference>), but are united to Christ, and admitted into communion with his church,—<hi type="italic">I Paul,</hi> who am <hi type="italic">the prisoner of Jesus Christ,</hi> pray that you may be enabled to act as becomes persons thus favoured by God, and made partakers of such privileges." To this purport you find him expressing himself in <reference osisRef="Eph.3.14">v. 14</reference>, where, after the digression contained in the several verses intervening, he proceeds with what he began in the <reference osisRef="Eph.3.1">first verse</reference>. Observe, Those who have received grace and signal favours from God stand in need of prayer, that they may improve and advance, and continue to act as becomes them. And, seeing Paul while he was a prisoner employed himself in such prayers to God in behalf of the Ephesians, we should learn that no particular sufferings of our own should make us so solicitous about ourselves as to neglect the cases of others in our supplications and addresses to God. He speaks again of his sufferings: <hi type="italic">Wherefore I desire that you faint not at my tribulation for you, which is your glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.13">v. 13</reference>. While he was in prison, he suffered much there; and, though it was upon their account that he suffered, yet he would not have them discouraged nor dismayed at this, seeing God had done such great things for them by his ministry. What a tender concern was here for these Ephesians! The apostle seems to have been more solicitous lest they should be discouraged and faint upon his tribulations than about what he himself endured; and, to prevent this, he tells them that his sufferings were their glory, and would be so far from being a real discouragement, if they duly considered the matter, that they ministered cause to them for glorying and for rejoicing, as this discovered the great esteem and regard which God bore to them, in that he not only sent his apostles to preach the gospel to them, but even to suffer for them, and to confirm the truths they delivered by the persecutions they underwent. Observe, Not only the faithful ministers of Christ themselves, but their people too, have some special cause for joy and glorying, when they suffer for the sake of dispensing the gospel. <div eID="gen31834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31835" type="x-p"/> II. The apostle informs them of God's appointing him to the office, and eminently fitting and qualifying him for it, by a special revelation that he made unto him. 1. God appointed him to the office: <hi type="italic">If you have heard of the dispensation of the grace of God, which is given me to you-ward,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.2">v. 2</reference>. They could not have heard of this, and therefore he does not design to speak doubtfully of this matter. <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Eige</hi></hi> is sometimes an affirmative particle, and we may read it, <hi type="italic">Since you have heard,</hi> &c. He styles the gospel <hi type="italic">the grace of God</hi> here (as in other places) because it is the gift of divine grace to sinful men; and all the gracious overtures that it makes, and the joyful tidings that it contains, proceed from the rich grace of God; and it is also the great instrument in the hands of the Spirit by which God works grace in the souls of men. He speaks of the dispensation of this grace given to him; he means as he was authorized and commissioned by God to dispense the doctrine of the gospel, which commission and authority were given to him chiefly for he service of the Gentiles: <hi type="italic">to you-ward.</hi> And again, speaking of the gospel, he says, <hi type="italic">Whereof I was made a minister,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Eph.3.7">v. 7</reference>. Here he again asserts his authority. He <hi type="italic">was</hi> <hi type="small-caps">made</hi> <hi type="italic">a minister</hi>—he did not make himself such; he took not to himself that honour—and he was made such <hi type="italic">according to the gift of the grace of God unto</hi> him. God supplied and furnished him for his work; and in the performance of it suitably assisted him with all needful gifts and graces, both ordinary and extraordinary, and that <hi type="italic">by the effectual working of his power,</hi> in himself more especially, and also in great numbers of those to whom he preached, by which means his labours among them were successful. Observe, What God calls men to he fits them for, and does it with an almighty power. An effectual working of divine power attends the gifts of divine grace. 2. As God appointed him to the office, so he eminently qualified him for it, by a special revelation that he made unto him. He makes mention both of the mystery that was revealed and of the revelation of it. (1.) The mystery revealed is <hi type="italic">that the Gentiles should be fellow-heirs, and of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ, by the gospel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.6">v. 6</reference>); that is, that they should be joint-heirs with the believing Jews of the heavenly inheritance; and that they should be members of the same mystical body, be received into the church of Christ, and be interested in the gospel-promises, as well as the Jews, and particularly in that great promise of the Spirit. And this <hi type="italic">in Christ,</hi> being united to Christ, <hi type="italic">in whom all the promises are yea and amen; and by the gospel,</hi> that is, in the times of the gospel, as some understand it; or, <hi type="italic">by the gospel</hi> preached to them, which is the great instrument and means by which God works faith in Christ, as others. This was the great truth revealed to the apostles, namely, that God would call the Gentiles to salvation by faith in Christ, and that without the works of the law. (2.) Of the revelation of this truth he speaks, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.3-Eph.3.5">v. 3-5</reference>. Here we may observe that the coalition of Jews and Gentiles in the gospel church was a mystery, a great mystery, what was designed in the counsel of God before all worlds, but what could not be fully understood for many ages, till the accomplishment expounded the prophecies of it. It is called a mystery because the several circumstances and peculiarities of it (such as the time and manner and means by which it should be effected) were concealed and kept secret in God's own breast, till be an immediate <hi type="italic">revelation he made them known</hi> to his servant. See <reference osisRef="Acts.26.16-Acts.26.18">Acts xxvi. 16-18</reference>. And it is called the mystery of Christ because it was revealed by him (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.12">Gal. i. 12</reference>), and because it relates so very much to him. Of this the apostle has given some hints <hi type="italic">afore,</hi> or a little before; that is, in the preceding chapters. <hi type="italic">Whereby, when you read;</hi> or, as those words may be read, <hi type="italic">unto which attending</hi> (and it is not enough for us barely to read the scriptures, unless we attend to them, and seriously consider and lay to heart what we read), <hi type="italic">you may understand my knowledge in the mystery of Christ;</hi> so as to perceive how God had fitted and qualified him to be an apostle to the Gentiles, which might be to them an evident token of his divine authority. <hi type="italic">This mystery,</hi> he says, <hi type="italic">in other ages was not made known unto the sons of men, as it is now revealed unto his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.5">v. 5</reference>); that is, "It was not so fully and clearly discovered in the ages before Christ as it is now revealed unto the prophets of this age, the prophets of the New Testament, who are immediately inspired and taught by the Spirit." Let us observe, that the conversion of the Gentile world to the faith of Christ was an adorable mystery, and we ought to bless God for it. Who would have imagined that those who had been so long in the dark, and at so great a distance, would be enlightened with the marvellous light, and be made nigh? Let us learn hence not to despair of the worst, of the worst of persons, and the worst of nations. Nothing is too hard for divine grace to do: none so unworthy but God may please to confer great grace upon them. And how much are we ourselves interested in this affair; not only as we live in a time in which the mystery is revealed, but particularly as we are a part of the nations which in times past were foreigners and strangers, and lived in gross idolatry; but are now enlightened with the everlasting gospel, and partake of its promises! <div eID="gen31835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31836" type="x-p"/> III. The apostle informs them how he was employed in this office, and that with respect to the Gentiles, and to all men. <div eID="gen31836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31837" type="x-p"/> 1. With respect to the Gentiles, he <hi type="italic">preached</hi> to them <hi type="italic">the unsearchable riches of Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.8">v. 8</reference>. Observe, in this verse, how humbly he speaks of himself, and how highly he speaks of Jesus Christ. (1.) How humbly he speaks of himself: <hi type="italic">I am less than the least of all saints.</hi> St. Paul, who was the chief of the apostles, calls himself <hi type="italic">less than the least of all saints:</hi> he means on account of his having been formerly a persecutor of the followers of Christ. He was, in his own esteem, as little as could be. What can be less than the least? To speak himself as little as could be, he speaks himself less than could be. Observe, Those whom God advances to honourable employments he humbles and makes low in their own eyes; and, where God gives grace to be humble, there he gives all other grace. You may also observe in what a different manner the apostle speaks of himself and of his office. While he magnifies his office, he debases himself. Observe, A faithful minister of Christ may be very humble, and think very meanly of himself, even when he thinks and speaks very highly and honourably of his sacred function. (2.) How highly he speaks of Jesus Christ: <hi type="italic">The unsearchable riches of Christ.</hi> There is a mighty treasury of mercy, grace, and love, laid up in Christ Jesus, and that both for Jews and Gentiles. Or, the riches of the gospel are here spoken of as the riches of Christ: the riches which Christ purchased for, and bestows upon, all believers. And they are unsearchable riches, which we cannot find the bottom of, which human sagacity could never have discovered, and men could no otherwise attain to the knowledge of them but by revelation. Now it was the apostle's business and employment to <hi type="italic">preach</hi> these <hi type="italic">unsearchable riches of Christ among the Gentiles:</hi> and it was a favour he greatly valued, and looked upon it as an unspeakable honour to him: "<hi type="italic">Unto me is this grace given;</hi> this special favour God has granted to such an unworthy creature as I am." And it is an unspeakable favour to the Gentile world that to them <hi type="italic">the unsearchable riches of Christ</hi> are preached. Though many remain poor, and are not enriched with these riches, yet it is a favour to have them preached among us, to have an offer of them made to us; and, if we are not enriched with them, it is our own fault. <div eID="gen31837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31838" type="x-p"/> 2. With respect to all men, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.9">v. 9</reference>. His business and employment were <hi type="italic">to make all men see</hi> (to publish and make known to the whole world) <hi type="italic">what is the fellowship of the mystery</hi> (that the Gentiles who have hitherto been strangers to the church, shall be admitted into communion with it) <hi type="italic">which from the beginning of the world hath been hid in God</hi> (kept secret in his purpose), <hi type="italic">who created all things by Jesus Christ:</hi> as <reference osisRef="John.1.3">John i. 3</reference>, <hi type="italic">All things were made by him, and without him was not any thing made that was made;</hi> and therefore no wonder that he saves the Gentiles as well as the Jews; for he is the common Creator of them both: and we may conclude that he is able to perform the work of their redemption, seeing he was able to accomplish the great work of creation. It is true that both the first creation, when God made all things out of nothing, and the new creation, whereby sinners are made new creatures by converting grace, are of God by Jesus Christ. The apostle adds, <hi type="italic">To the intent that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known, by the church, the manifold wisdom of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.10">v. 10</reference>. This was one things, among others, which God had in his eye in revealing this mystery, that the good angels, who have a pre-eminence in governing the kingdoms and principalities of the world, and who are endued with great power to execute the will of God on this earth (though their ordinary residence is in heaven) may be informed, from what passes in the church and is done in and by it, <hi type="italic">of the manifold wisdom of God;</hi> that is, of the great variety with which God wisely dispenses things, or of his wisdom manifested in the many ways and methods he takes in ordering his church in the several ages of it, and especially in receiving the Gentiles into it. The holy angels, who look into the mystery of our redemption by Christ, could not but take notice of this branch of that mystery, that among the Gentiles is preached the unsearchable riches of Christ. And this is <hi type="italic">according to the eternal purpose which he purposed in Christ Jesus our Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.11">v. 11</reference>. Some translate the words <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kata prothesin ton aionon</hi></hi> thus <hi type="italic">According to the fore-disposing of the ages which he made,</hi> &c. So Dr. Whitby, &c. "In the first of the ages," says this author, "his wisdom seeing fit to give the promise of a Saviour to a fallen Adam: in the second age to typify and represent him to the Jews in sacred persons, rites, and sacrifices: and in the age of the Messiah, or the last age, to reveal him to the Jews, and preach him to the Gentiles." Others understand it, according to our translation, of the eternal purpose which God purposed to execute in and through Jesus Christ, the whole of what he has done in the great affair of man's redemption being in pursuance of his eternal decree about that matter. The apostle, having mentioned our Lord Jesus Christ, subjoins concerning him, <hi type="italic">In whom we have boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.12">v. 12</reference>); that is, "By (or through) whom we have liberty to open our minds freely to God, as to a Father, and a well-grounded persuasion of audience and of acceptance with him; and this by means of the faith we have in him, as our great Mediator and Advocate." We may come with humble boldness to hear from God, knowing that the terror of the curse is done away; and we may expect to hear from him good words and comfortable. We may have access with confidence to speak to God, knowing that we have such a Mediator between God and us, and such an Advocate with the Father.
entries.34a2fad6f7f557269d90fe8620826eabe963f612: <div eID="gen31838" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Prayer. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 61.)</title> <div sID="gen31839" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> For this cause I bow my knees unto the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, <hi type="super">15</hi> Of whom the whole family in heaven and earth is named, <hi type="super">16</hi> That he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man; <hi type="super">17</hi> That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith; that ye, being rooted and grounded in love, 18 May be able to comprehend with all saints what <hi type="italic">is</hi> the breadth, and length, and depth, and height; <hi type="super">19</hi> And to know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge, that ye might be filled with all the fulness of God. <hi type="super">20</hi> Now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us, <hi type="super">21</hi> Unto him <hi type="italic">be</hi> glory in the church by Christ Jesus throughout all ages, world without end. Amen. <div eID="gen31839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31840" type="x-p"/> We now come to the second part of this chapter, which contains Paul's devout and affectionate prayer to God for his beloved Ephesians.—<hi type="italic">For this cause.</hi> This may be referred either to the immediately <reference osisRef="Eph.3.13">foregoing verse</reference>, <hi type="italic">That you faint not,</hi> &c., or, rather, the apostle is here resuming what he began at the <reference osisRef="Eph.3.1">first verse</reference>, from which he digressed in those which are interposed. Observe, <div eID="gen31840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31841" type="x-p"/> I. To whom he prays—to God, as <hi type="italic">the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,</hi> of which see <reference osisRef="Eph.1.3">ch. i. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen31841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31842" type="x-p"/> II. His outward posture in prayer, which was humble and reverent: <hi type="italic">I bow my knees.</hi> Note, When we draw nigh to God, we should reverence him in our hearts, and express our reverence in the most suitable and becoming behaviour and gesture. Here, having mentioned Christ, he cannot pass without an honourable encomium of his love, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.15">v. 15</reference>. The universal church has a dependence upon the Lord Jesus Christ: <hi type="italic">Of whom the whole family in heaven and earth is named.</hi> The Jews were wont to boast of Abraham as their father, but now Jews and Gentiles are both denominated from Christ (so some); while others understand it of the saints in heaven, who wear the crown of glory, and of saints on earth who are going on in the work of grace here. Both the one and the other make but one family, one household; and from him they are <hi type="italic">named</hi> <hi type="small-caps">Christians</hi> , as they really are such, acknowledging their dependence upon, and their relation to, Christ. <div eID="gen31842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31843" type="x-p"/> III. What the apostle asks of God for these his friends—spiritual blessings, which are the best blessings, and the most earnestly to be sought and prayed for by every one of us, both for ourselves and for our friends. 1. Spiritual strength for the work and duty to which they were called, and in which they were employed: <hi type="italic">That he would grant you, according to the riches of his grace, to be strengthened,</hi> &c. <hi type="italic">The inner man</hi> is the heart or soul. To be <hi type="italic">strengthened with might</hi> is to be mightily strengthened, much more than they were at present; to be endued with a high degree of grace, and spiritual abilities for discharging duty, resisting temptations, enduring persecutions, &c. And the apostle prays that this may be <hi type="italic">according to the riches of his glory,</hi> or according to his glorious riches—answerable to that great abundance of grace, mercy, and power, which resides in God, and is his glory: and this by his Spirit, who is the immediate worker of grace in the souls of God's people. Observe from these things, That strength from the Spirit of God in the inner man is the best and most desirable strength, strength in the soul, the strength of faith and other graces, strength to serve God and to do our duty, and to persevere in our Christian course with vigour and with cheerfulness. And let us further observe that <hi type="italic">as the work of grace is first begun so it is continued and carried on, by the blessed Spirit of God.</hi> 2. The indwelling of Christ in their hearts, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.17">v. 17</reference>. Christ is said to dwell in his people, as he is always present with them by his gracious influences and operations. Observe, It is a desirable thing to have Christ dwell in our hearts; and if the law of Christ be written there, and the love of Christ be shed abroad there, then Christ dwells there. Christ is an inhabitant in the soul of every good Christian. Where his spirit dwells, there he swells; and he dwells in the heart by faith, by means of the continual exercise of faith upon him. Faith opens the door of the soul, to receive Christ; faith admits him, and submits to him. By faith we are united to Christ, and have an interest in him. 3. The fixing of pious and devout affections in the soul: <hi type="italic">That you being rooted and grounded in love,</hi> stedfastly fixed in your love to God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to all the saints, the beloved of our Lord Jesus Christ. Many have some love to God and to his servants, but it is a flash, like the crackling of thorns under a pot, it makes a great noise, but is gone presently. We should earnestly desire that good affections may be fixed in us, that we may be <hi type="italic">rooted and grounded in love.</hi> Some understand it of their being settled and established in the sense of God's love to them, which would inspire them with greater ardours of holy love to him, and to one another. And how very desirable is it to have a settled fixed sense of the love of God and Christ to our souls, so as to be able to say with the apostle at all times, <hi type="italic">He has loved me!</hi> Now the best way to attain this is to be careful that we maintain a constant love to God in our souls; this will be the evidence of the love of God to us. <hi type="italic">We love him, because he first loved us.</hi> In order to this he prays, 4. For their experimental acquaintance with the love of Jesus Christ. The more intimate acquaintance we have with Christ's love to us, the more our love will be drawn out to him, and to those who are his, for his sake: <hi type="italic">That you may be able to comprehend with all saints,</hi> &c. (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.18-Eph.3.19">v. 18, 19</reference>); that is, more clearly to understand, and firmly to believe, the wonderful love of Christ to his, which the saints do understand and believe in some measure, and shall understand more hereafter. Christians should not aim to comprehend above all saints; but be content that God deals with them as he uses to do with those who love and fear his name: we should desire to comprehend <hi type="italic">with all saints,</hi> to have so much knowledge as the saints are allowed to have in this world. We should be ambitious of coming up with <hi type="italic">the first three;</hi> but not of going beyond what is the measure of the stature of other saints. It is observable how magnificently the apostle speaks of the love of Christ. The dimensions of redeeming love are admirable: <hi type="italic">The breadth, and length, and depth, and height.</hi> By enumerating these dimensions, the apostle designs to signify the exceeding greatness of the love of Christ, the unsearchable riches of his love, which is <hi type="italic">higher than heaven, deeper than hell, longer than the earth, and broader than the sea,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.11.8-Job.11.9">Job xi. 8, 9</reference>. Some describe the particulars thus: By the breadth of it we may understand the extent of it to all ages, nations, and ranks of men; by the length of it, its continuance from everlasting to everlasting; by the depth of it, its stooping to the lowest condition, with a design to relieve and save those who have sunk into the depths of sin and misery; by its height, its entitling and raising us up to the heavenly happiness and glory. We should desire to comprehend this love: it is the character of all the saints that they do so; for they all have a complacency and a confidence in the love of Christ: <hi type="italic">And to know the love of Christ which passeth knowledge,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.19">v. 19</reference>. If it passeth knowledge, how can we know it? We must pray and endeavour to know something, and should still covet and strive to know more and more of it, though, after the best endeavours, none can fully comprehend it: in its full extent it surpasses knowledge. Though the love of Christ may be better perceived and known by Christians than it generally is, yet it cannot be fully understood on this side heaven. 5. He prays that they may <hi type="italic">be filled with all the fulness of God.</hi> It is a high expression: we should not dare to use it if we did not find it in the scriptures. It is like those other expressions, of being <hi type="italic">partakers of a divine nature,</hi> and of being <hi type="italic">perfect as our Father in heaven is perfect.</hi> We are not to understand it of his fulness as God in himself, but of his fulness as a God in covenant with us, as a God to his people: such a fulness as God is ready to bestow, who is willing to fill them all to the utmost of their capacity, and that with all those gifts and graces which he sees they need. Those who receive grace for grace from Christ's fulness may be said to be <hi type="italic">filled with the fulness of God,</hi> according to their capacity, all which is in order to their arriving at the highest degree of the knowledge and enjoyment of God, and an entire conformity to him. <div eID="gen31843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31844" type="x-p"/> The apostle closes the chapter with a doxology, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.20-Eph.3.21">v. 20, 21</reference>. It is proper to conclude our prayers with praises. Our blessed Saviour has taught us to do so. Take notice how he describes God, and how he ascribes glory to him. He describes him as a God that <hi type="italic">is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think.</hi> There is an inexhaustible fulness of grace and mercy in God, which the prayers of all the saints can never draw dry. Whatever we may ask, or think to ask, still God is still able to do more, abundantly more, exceedingly abundantly more. Open thy mouth ever so wide, still he hath wherewithal to fill it. Note, In our applications to God we should encourage our faith by a consideration of his all-sufficiency and almighty power. <hi type="italic">According to the power which worketh in us.</hi> As if he had said, We have already had a proof of this power of God, in what he hath wrought in us and done for us, having quickened us by his grace, and converted us to himself. The power that still worketh for the saints is according to that power that hath wrought in them. Wherever God gives of his fulness he gives to experience his power. Having thus described God, he ascribes glory to him. When we come to ask for grace from God, we ought to give glory to God. Unto him be glory in the church by Christ Jesus. In ascribing glory to God, we ascribe all excellences and perfections to him, glory being the effulgency and result of them all. Observe, The seat of God's praises is in the church. That little rent of praise which God receives from this world is from the church, a sacred society constituted for the glory of God, every particular member of which, both Jew and Gentile, concurs in this work of praising God. The Mediator of these praises is Jesus Christ. All God's gifts come from his to us through the hand of Christ; and all our praises pass from us to him through the same hand. And God should and will be praised thus <hi type="italic">throughout all ages, world without end;</hi> for he will ever have a church to praise him, and he will ever have his tribute of praise from his church. <hi type="italic">Amen.</hi> So be it; and so it will certainly be.  <chapter eID="Eph.3"/> <div eID="gen31844" type="x-p"/>

entries.5e58c52f7528bbd91e0dc23efc202bda127fe2e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17616"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Eph.3.1-Eph.3.21">Ep 3:1-21</reference>. His Apostolic Office to Make Known the Mystery of Christ Revealed by the Spirit: Prayer that by the Same Spirit They May Comprehend the Vast Love of Christ: Doxology Ending This Division of the Epistle.</title> <div sID="gen35522" type="x-p"/> As the first chapter treated of THE Father's office; and the second, THE Son's, so this, that of THE Spirit.<div eID="gen35522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35523" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17616"/><hi type="bold">1. of Jesus Christ--</hi>Greek, "Christ Jesus." The office is the prominent thought in the latter arrangement; the person, in the former. He here marks the Messiahship of "Christ," maintained by him as the origin of his being a "prisoner," owing to the jealousy of the Jews being roused at his preaching it to the Gentiles. His very bonds were profitable to ("for" or "in behalf of you") Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.13">Ep 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.10">2Ti 2:10</reference>). He digresses at "For this cause," and does not complete the sentence which he had intended, until <reference osisRef="Eph.3.14">Ep 3:14</reference>, where he resumes the words, "For this cause," namely, because I know this your call of God as Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.11-Eph.2.22">Ep 2:11-22</reference>), to be "fellow-heirs" with the Jews (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.6">Ep 3:6</reference>), "I bow my knees to" the Father of our common Saviour (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.14">Ep 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.15">15</reference>) to confirm you in the faith by His Spirit. "I Paul," expresses the agent employed by the Spirit to enlighten them, after he had been first enlightened himself by the same Spirit (Ep 3:3-5, 9). <div eID="gen35523" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5c67d461e019136ad37a0b496059faa98a91a18: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17617"/><div sID="gen35524" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17617"/><hi type="bold">2. If--</hi>The Greek does not imply doubt: "Assuming (what I know to be the fact, namely) that ye have heard," &c. "If, as I presume," The indicative in the Greek shows that no doubt is implied: "Seeing that doubtless," &c. He by this phrase delicately reminds them of their having heard from himself, and probably from others subsequently, the fact. See Introduction, showing that these words do not disprove the address of this Epistle to the Ephesians. Compare <reference osisRef="Acts.20.17-Acts.20.24">Ac 20:17-24</reference>.<div eID="gen35524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35525" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the dispensation--</hi>"The office of dispensing, as a steward, the grace of God which was (not 'is') given me to you-ward," namely, to dispense to you. <div eID="gen35525" type="x-p"/>
entries.b27e97ad7701c0cc00b58b6039740966512137a4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17618"/><div sID="gen35526" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17618"/><hi type="bold">3. he made known--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "That by revelation was the mystery (namely, of the admission of the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.6">Ep 3:6</reference>; 1:9) made known unto me (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.12">Ga 1:12</reference>)."<div eID="gen35526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35527" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as I wrote afore--</hi>namely, in this Epistle (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.9">Ep 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>), the words of which he partly repeats. <div eID="gen35527" type="x-p"/>
entries.ee18255b40484bcc3e393c772299ef60bba4f710: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17619"/><div sID="gen35528" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17619"/><hi type="bold">4. understand my knowledge--</hi>"perceive my understanding" [Alford], or "intelligence." "When ye read," implies that, deep as are the mysteries of this Epistle, the way for all to understand them is to read it (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.15">2Ti 3:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.16">16</reference>). By perceiving his understanding of the mysteries, they, too, will be enabled to understand.<div eID="gen35528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35529" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the mystery of Christ--</hi>The "mystery" is Christ Himself, once hidden, but now revealed (<reference osisRef="Col.1.27">Col 1:27</reference>). <div eID="gen35529" type="x-p"/>
entries.4227cb21bd7dd8acf40a84cd3c1e718a8771dfe2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17620"/><div sID="gen35530" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17620"/><hi type="bold">5. in other ages--</hi>Greek, "generations."<div eID="gen35530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35531" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not made known--</hi>He does not say, "has not been revealed." Making known by revelation is the source of making known by preaching [Bengel]. The former was vouchsafed only to the prophets, in order that they might make known the truth so revealed to men in general.<div eID="gen35531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35532" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the sons of men--</hi>men in their state by birth, as contrasted with those illuminated "by the Spirit" (Greek, "IN the Spirit," compare <reference osisRef="Rev.1.10">Re 1:10</reference>), <reference osisRef="Matt.16.17">Mt 16:17</reference>.<div eID="gen35532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35533" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as--</hi>The mystery of the call of the Gentiles (of which Paul speaks here) was not unknown to the Old Testament prophets (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.6">Is 56:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.6">49:6</reference>). But they did not know it with the same explicit distinctness "As" it has been now known (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.19">Ac 10:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.10.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.11.18-Acts.11.21">11:18-21</reference>). They probably did not know that the Gentiles were to be admitted without circumcision or that they were to be on a level with the Jews in partaking of the grace of God. The gift of "the Spirit" in its fulness was reserved for the New Testament that Christ might thereby be glorified. The epithet, "holy," marks the special consecration of the New Testament "prophets" (who are here meant) by the Spirit, compared with which even the Old Testament prophets were but "sons of men" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.2.3">Eze 2:3</reference>, and elsewhere). <div eID="gen35533" type="x-p"/>
entries.e136651c7a2f1d93e85c23871dcdf85386fa6098: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17621"/><div sID="gen35534" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17621"/>6. Translate, "That the Gentiles are," &c. "and fellow members of the same body, and fellow partakers of the (so the oldest manuscripts read, not 'His') promise, in Christ Jesus (added in the oldest manuscripts), through the Gospel." It is "in Christ Jesus" that they are made "fellow heirs" in the inheritance of God: "of the same body" under the Head, Christ Jesus; and "fellow partakers of the promise" in the communion of THE Holy Spirit (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.13">Ep 1:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.4">He 6:4</reference>). The Trinity is thus alluded to, as often elsewhere in this Epistle (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.19">Ep 2:19</reference>, 20, 22). <div eID="gen35534" type="x-p"/>
entries.b6d0ab968ca68593f10ccafd033cc34f7f2706bf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17622"/><div sID="gen35535" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17622"/><hi type="bold">7. Whereof--</hi>"of which" Gospel.<div eID="gen35535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35536" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to--</hi>in consequence of, and in accordance with, "the gift of the grace of God."<div eID="gen35536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35537" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">given--</hi>"which (gift of grace) was given to me by (Greek, 'according to,' as in <reference osisRef="Eph.3.20">Ep 3:20</reference>; 1:19: as the result of, and in proportion to) the effectual working (Greek, 'energy,' or 'in-working') of His power." <div eID="gen35537" type="x-p"/>
entries.abb237953e92bbbb519e7c494677cbd882327cfa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17623"/><div sID="gen35538" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17623"/><hi type="bold">8. am--</hi>Not merely was I in times past, but I still am the least worthy of so high an office (compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.15">1Ti 1:15</reference>, end).<div eID="gen35538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35539" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">least of all saints--</hi>not merely "of all apostles" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.9">1Co 15:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.10">10</reference>).<div eID="gen35539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35540" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is--</hi>Greek, "has been given."<div eID="gen35540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35541" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts Translate, "to announce to the Gentiles the glad tidings of the unsearchable (<reference osisRef="Job.5.9">Job 5:9</reference>) riches," namely, of Christ's grace (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.7">Ep 1:7</reference>; 2:7). <reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">Ro 11:33</reference>, "unsearchable" as a mine inexhaustible, whose treasures can never be fully explored (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.18">Ep 3:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.19">19</reference>). <div eID="gen35541" type="x-p"/>
entries.141063c9786a3c795db3cc6cb81c87dfa6b87159: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17624"/><div sID="gen35542" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17624"/><hi type="bold">9. to make all men see--</hi>Greek, "to enlighten all" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.18">Ep 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.28">Psa 18:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.4">He 6:4</reference>). "All" (compare <reference osisRef="Col.1.28">Col 1:28</reference>).<div eID="gen35542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35543" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fellowship--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "economy," or "dispensation" (compare <reference osisRef="Col.1.25">Col 1:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.26">26</reference>; and see on <reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Ep 1:10</reference>, above). "To make all see how it hath seemed good to God at this time to dispense (through me and others, His stewards) what heretofore was a mystery." Ellicott explains it, "the arrangement," or "regulation" of the mystery (the union of Jews and Gentiles in Christ) which was now to be humbly traced and acknowledged in the fact of its having secretly existed in the counsel of God, and now having been revealed to the heavenly powers by means of the Church.<div eID="gen35543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35544" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the beginning of the world--</hi>Greek, "from (the beginning of) the ages." Compare <reference osisRef="Eph.1.4">Ep 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.16.25">Ro 16:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7">1Co 2:7</reference>. The "ages" are the vast successive periods of time, marked by successive stages of creation and orders of beings.<div eID="gen35544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35545" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in God--</hi>"hidden in" His counsels (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.9">Ep 1:9</reference>).<div eID="gen35545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35546" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">created all things by Jesus Christ--</hi>God's creation of the world and all things therein is the foundation of the rest of the "economy," which is freely dispensed according to the universal power of God [Bengel]. AS God created "the whole range of things" (so the Greek), physical and spiritual alike, He must have an absolute right to adjust all things as He will. Hence, we may see His right to keep the mystery of world-wide salvation in Christ "hidden in Himself," till his own good time for revealing it. The oldest manuscripts omit "by Jesus Christ." <div eID="gen35546" type="x-p"/>
entries.124adf6ee557924fd1f0f03927c1efaf85a06abd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17625"/><div sID="gen35547" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17625"/>10. The design of God in giving Paul grace to proclaim to the Gentiles the mystery of salvation heretofore hidden.<div eID="gen35547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35548" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">now--</hi>first: opposed to "hidden from the beginning of the world" (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.5">Ep 3:5</reference>).<div eID="gen35548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35549" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the principalities and--</hi>Greek adds "the"<div eID="gen35549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35550" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">powers--</hi>unto the various orders of good angels primarily, as these dwell "in the heavenly places" in the highest sense; "known" to their adoring joy (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.12">1Pe 1:12</reference>). Secondarily, God's wisdom in redemption is made known to evil angels, who dwell "in heavenly places" in a lower sense, namely, the air (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Ep 2:2</reference> with <reference osisRef="Eph.6.12">Ep 6:12</reference>); "known" to their dismay (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.24">1Co 15:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.15">Col 2:15</reference>).<div eID="gen35550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35551" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">might be known--</hi>Translate, "may be known."<div eID="gen35551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35552" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the church--</hi>"by means of," or "through the Church," which is the "theater" for the display of God's manifold wisdom (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.10">Lu 15:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.9">1Co 4:9</reference>): "a spectacle (Greek, 'theater') to angels." Hence, angels are but our "fellow servants" (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.10">Re 19:10</reference>).<div eID="gen35552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35553" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">manifold wisdom--</hi>though essentially one, as Christ is one, yet varying the economy in respect to places, times, and persons (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.8">Is 55:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.1">He 1:1</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.10">1Pe 4:10</reference>, "stewards of the manifold grace of God." Man cannot understand aright its single acts till he can survey them as a connected whole (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.12">1Co 13:12</reference>). The call of the Church is no haphazard remedy, or afterthought, but part of the eternal scheme, which, amidst manifold varieties of dispensation, is one in its end. <div eID="gen35553" type="x-p"/>
entries.901e46b9455898c1f0ffb770270f9f52b31ba635: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17626"/><div sID="gen35554" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17626"/><hi type="bold">11. which he purposed--</hi>Greek, "made." Ellicott translates, "wrought." <div eID="gen35554" type="x-p"/>
entries.06c6fe53994c0471a0939382cfbaf51687925b6a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17627"/><div sID="gen35555" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17627"/>12. Translate, "our boldness and our access (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.18">Ep 2:18</reference>) in confidence through our faith in Him." Alford quotes as an instance, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.38">Ro 8:38</reference>, &c. "THE access" (Greek) implies the formal introduction into the presence of a monarch. <div eID="gen35555" type="x-p"/>
entries.525c49ee7cba2d8a28b77e3e409bff428c034ebe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17628"/><div sID="gen35556" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17628"/>13. "I entreat you not to be dispirited."<div eID="gen35556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35557" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for you--</hi>in your behalf.<div eID="gen35557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35558" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which is--</hi>rather, "which are your glory," namely, inasmuch as showing that God loved you so much, as both to give His Son for you, and to permit His apostles to suffer "tribulations" for you [Chrysostom] in preaching the Gospel to the Gentiles. See on <reference osisRef="Eph.3.1">Ep 3:1</reference>, "prisoner for you Gentiles." My tribulations are your spiritual "glory," as your faith is furthered thereby (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.10">1Co 4:10</reference>). <div eID="gen35558" type="x-p"/>
entries.665f53f08e40de9a5f2cee97fed12b3786e45180: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17629"/><div sID="gen35559" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17629"/><hi type="bold">14. For this cause--</hi>Resuming the thread of <reference osisRef="Eph.3.1">Ep 3:1</reference>, "For this cause." Because ye have such a standing in God's Church [Alford].<div eID="gen35559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35560" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bow my knees--</hi>the proper attitude in humble prayer. Posture affects the mind, and is not therefore unimportant. See Paul's practice (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.36">Ac 20:36</reference>); and that of the Lord Himself on earth (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.41">Lu 22:41</reference>).<div eID="gen35560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35561" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the Father--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "of our Lord Jesus Christ." But Vulgate and some very old authorities retain them: <reference osisRef="Eph.3.15">Ep 3:15</reference>, "From whom," in either case, refers to "the Father" (Patera), as "family" (patria, akin in sound and etymology) plainly refers to Him. Still the foundation of all sonship is in Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen35561" type="x-p"/>
entries.33bc68495bbb9d61e7ca3fd6522e1aa9d821c17d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17630"/><div sID="gen35562" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17630"/><hi type="bold">15. the whole family--</hi>Alford, Middleton, and others translate, "every family": alluding to the several families in heaven and in earth supposed to exist [Theophylact, Æcumenius, in Suicer, 2.633], the apostle thus being supposed to imply that God, in His relation of Father to us His adopted children, is the great prototype of the paternal relation wherever found. But the idea that "the holy angels are bound up in spiritual families or compaternities," is nowhere else in Scripture referred to. And <reference osisRef="Acts.2.36">Ac 2:36</reference>, where the article is similarly omitted, and yet the translation is, "All the house of Israel," shows that in New Testament Greek the translation is justifiable, "all the family," or "the whole family": which accords with Scripture views, that angels and men, the saints militant and those with God, are one holy family joined under the one Father in Christ, the mediator between heaven and earth (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Ep 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.10">Php 2:10</reference>). Hence angels are termed our "brethren" (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.10">Re 19:10</reference>), and "sons of God" by creation, as we are by adoption (<reference osisRef="Job.38.7">Job 38:7</reference>). The Church is part of the grand family, or kingdom, which comprehends, besides men, the higher spiritual world, where the archetype, to the realization of which redeemed man is now tending, is already realized. This universal idea of the "kingdom" of God as one divine community, is presented to us in the Lord's Prayer. By sin men were estranged, not only from God, but from that higher spiritual world in which the kingdom of God is already realized. As Christ when He reconciled men to God, united them to one another in a divine community (joined to Himself, the one Head), breaking down the partition wall between Jew and Gentile (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.14">Ep 2:14</reference>), so also He joins them in communion with all those who have already attained that perfection in the kingdom of God, to which the Church on earth is aspiring (<reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>) [Neander].<div eID="gen35562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35563" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is named--</hi>derives its origin and its name as sons of God. To be named, and to be, are one with God. To bear God's name is to belong to God as His own peculiar people (<reference osisRef="Num.6.27">Nu 6:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.7">Is 43:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.5">44:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.25">Ro 9:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.26">26</reference>). <div eID="gen35563" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b62a409b9959719e85db73529342439c9a127cf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17631"/><div sID="gen35564" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17631"/><hi type="bold">16. according to--</hi>that is in abundance consonant to the riches of His glory; not "according to" the narrowness of our hearts. <reference osisRef="Col.1.11">Col 1:11</reference>, "Strengthened with all might according to His glorious power."<div eID="gen35564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35565" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by--</hi>Greek, "through"; "by means of His Spirit."<div eID="gen35565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35566" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in--</hi>The Greek implies, "infused into."<div eID="gen35566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35567" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the inner man--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.4.22">Ep 4:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.4">1Pe 3:4</reference>); "the hidden man of the heart." Not predicated of unbelievers, whose inward and outward man alike are carnal. But in believers, the "inner (new) man," their true self, stands in contrast to their old man, which is attached to them as a body of death daily being mortified, but not their true self. <div eID="gen35567" type="x-p"/>
entries.13083603d91bea3022567856ab73fa961378afba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17632"/><div sID="gen35568" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17632"/><hi type="bold">17. That--</hi>So that.<div eID="gen35568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35569" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dwell--</hi>abidingly make His abode (<reference osisRef="John.14.23">Joh 14:23</reference>). Where the Spirit is there Christ is (<reference osisRef="John.14.16">Joh 14:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.14.18">18</reference>).<div eID="gen35569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35570" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by faith--</hi>Greek, "through faith," which opens the door of the heart to Jesus (<reference osisRef="John.3.20">Joh 3:20</reference>). It is not enough that He be on the tongue, or flit through the brain: the heart is His proper seat [Calvin]. "You being rooted and grounded in love" (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.3.19">Ep 3:19</reference>), is in the Greek connected with this clause, not with the clause, "that ye may be able to comprehend." "Rooted" is an image from a tree; "grounded" (Greek, "founder," "having your foundations resting on"), from a building (compare Notes,, see on <reference osisRef="Eph.2.20">Ep 2:20</reference>,21; <reference osisRef="Col.1.23">Col 1:23</reference>; 2:7). Contrast <reference osisRef="Matt.13.6">Mt 13:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.21">21</reference>. "Love," the first-fruit of the Spirit, flowing from Christ's love realized in the soul, was to be the basis on which should rest their further comprehension of all the vastness of Christ's love. <div eID="gen35570" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce1dd240bb0dbb82cbbb6ccfd2637deec947f1c8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17633"/><div sID="gen35571" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17633"/><hi type="bold">18. May be able--</hi>even still further. Greek, "May be fully able."<div eID="gen35571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35572" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">breadth ... length ... depth ... height--</hi>namely, the full dimensions of the spiritual temple, answering to "the fulness of God" (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.19">Ep 3:19</reference>), to which the Church, according to its capacity, ought to correspond (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.4.10">Ep 4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.13">13</reference>) as to "the fulness of Christ." The "breadth" implies Christ's world-wide love, embracing all men: the "length," its being extended through all ages (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.21">Ep 3:21</reference>); the "depth," its profound wisdom which no creature can fathom (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">Ro 11:33</reference>); the "height," its being beyond the reach of any foe to deprive us of (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.8">Ep 4:8</reference>) [Bengel]. I prefer to understand "the breadth," &c., to refer to the whole of the vast mystery of free salvation in Christ for all, Gentile and Jew alike, of which Paul had been speaking (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.3-Eph.3.9">Ep 3:3-9</reference>), and of which he now prays they may have a fuller comprehension. As subsidiary to this, and the most essential part of it, he adds, "and to know the love of Christ" (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.19">Ep 3:19</reference>). Grotius understands depth and height of God's goodness raising us from the lowest depression to the greatest height. <div eID="gen35572" type="x-p"/>
entries.f8102910decb9aa31122f4cb8b9f937dce16db01: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17634"/><div sID="gen35573" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17634"/><hi type="bold">19. passeth--</hi>surpasseth, exceeds. The paradox "to know ... which passeth knowledge," implies that when he says "know," he does not mean that we can adequately know; all we know is, that His love exceeds far our knowledge of it, and with even our fresh accessions of knowledge hereafter, will still exceed them. Even as God's power exceeds our thoughts (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.20">Ep 3:20</reference>).<div eID="gen35573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35574" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">filled with--</hi>rather, as Greek, "filled even unto all the fulness of God" (this is the grand goal), that is, filled, each according to your capacity, with the divine wisdom, knowledge, and love; "even as God is full," and as Christ who dwells in your hearts, hath "all the fulness of the Godhead dwelling in Him bodily" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.9">Col 2:9</reference>). <div eID="gen35574" type="x-p"/>
entries.358ff6bb7e6576b2d6618e82f2fd697299d55ad9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17635"/><div sID="gen35575" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17635"/><hi type="bold">20. unto him--</hi>contrasted with ourselves and our needs. Translate, "that is able above all things (what is above all things) to do exceeding abundantly above what we ask or (even) think": thought takes a wider range than prayers. The word, above, occurs thrice as often in Paul's writings, as in all the rest of the New Testament, showing the warm exuberance of Paul's spirit.<div eID="gen35575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35576" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to the power--</hi>the indwelling Spirit (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.26">Ro 8:26</reference>). He appeals to their and his experience. 21. Translate, "Unto Him be the glory (that is, the whole glory of the gracious dispensation of salvation just spoken of) in the Church (as the theater for the manifestation of the glory, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.10">Ep 3:10</reference>) in Christ Jesus (as in Him all the glory centers, <reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">Zec 6:13</reference>) to all the generations of eternal ages," literally, "of the age of the ages." Eternity is conceived as consisting of "ages" (these again consisting of "generations") endlessly succeeding one another. <chapter eID="Eph.3"/>

entries.2002334e801b446722817ed5b3491df60f0bad18: <div eID="gen50080" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen50081" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen50082" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen50082" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen50081" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen50083" type="x-p"/> Paul, a prisoner for the testimony of Jesus, declares his knowledge of what had been a mystery from all ages, that the Gentiles should be fellow heirs and of the same body with the Jews, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.1-Eph.3.6">Eph 3:1-6</reference>. Which doctrine he was made a minister, that he might declare the unsearchable riches of Christ, and make known to principalities and powers this eternal purpose of God, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.7-Eph.3.12">Eph 3:7-12</reference>. He desires them not to be discouraged on account of his tribulations, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.13">Eph 3:13</reference>. His prayer that they might be filled with all the fullness of God, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.14-Eph.3.19">Eph 3:14-19</reference>. His doxology, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.20">Eph 3:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.21">Eph 3:21</reference>. <div eID="gen50083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50084" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen50084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50085" type="x-p"/> For this cause - Because he maintained that the Gentiles were admitted to all the privileges of the Jews, and all the blessings of the new covenant, without being obliged to submit to circumcision, the Jews persecuted him, and caused him to be imprisoned, first at Caesarea, where he was obliged to appeal to the Roman emperor, in consequence of which he was sent prisoner to Rome. See <reference osisRef="Act.21.21-Act.21.28">Act 21:21-28</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen50085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50086" type="x-p"/> The prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles - For preaching the Gospel to the Gentiles, and showing that they were not bound by the law of Moses, and yet were called to be fellow citizens with the saints; for this very cause the Jews persecuted him unto bonds, and conspired his death.
entries.8da6bb84bf6ea3ffb79ab71c37739d942b49e180: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen50086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50087" type="x-p"/> If ye have heard of the dispensation - The compound particle ειγε, which is commonly translated if indeed, in several places means since indeed, seeing that, and should be translated so in this verse, and in several other places of the New Testament. Seeing ye have heard of the dispensation of God, which is given me to you-ward: this they had amply learned from the apostle during his stay at Ephesus, for he had not shunned to declare unto them the whole counsel of God, <reference osisRef="Act.20.27">Act 20:27</reference>, and kept nothing back that was profitable to them, <reference osisRef="Act.20.20">Act 20:20</reference>. And this was certainly among those things that were most profitable, and most necessary to be known. <div eID="gen50087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50088" type="x-p"/> By the dispensation of the grace of God we may understand, either the apostolic office and gifts granted to St. Paul, for the purpose of preaching the Gospel among the Gentiles, see <reference osisRef="Rom.1.5">Rom 1:5</reference>; or the knowledge which God gave him of that gracious and Divine plan which he had formed for the conversion of the Gentiles. For the meaning of the word economy see the note on <reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Eph 1:10</reference>.
entries.5229c45021ae3cde6c9fa6df8dc51dcb12148822: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen50088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50089" type="x-p"/> By revelation he made known unto me - Instead of εγνωρισε, he made known, εγνωρισθη, was made known, is the reading of ABCD*FG, several others, both the Syriac, Coptic, Slavonic, Vulgate, and Itala, with Clemens, Cyril, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Damascenus, and others: it is doubtless the true reading. <div eID="gen50089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50090" type="x-p"/> The apostle wishes the Ephesians to understand that it was not an opinion of his own, or a doctrine which he was taught by others, or which he had gathered from the ancient prophets; but one that came to him by immediate revelation from God, as he had informed them before in a few words, referring to what he had said <reference osisRef="Eph.1.9-Eph.1.12">Eph 1:9-12</reference>.
entries.b796262f92e7c30c577a681ff04292fb6eeab727: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen50090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50091" type="x-p"/> Whereby, when ye read - When ye refer back to them. <div eID="gen50091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50092" type="x-p"/> Ye may understand my knowledge - Ye may see what God has given me to know concerning what has been hitherto a mystery - the calling of the Gentiles, and the breaking down the middle wall between them and the Jews, so as to make both one spiritual body, and on the same conditions.
entries.83ebf41859b0650da422738c1a698bb24be69f7f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen50092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50093" type="x-p"/> Which in other ages was not made known - That the calling of the Gentiles was made known by the prophets in different ages of the Jewish Church is exceedingly clear; but it certainly was not made known in that clear and precise manner in which it was now revealed by the Spirit unto the ministers of the New Testament: nor was it made known unto them at all, that the Gentiles should find salvation without coming under the yoke of the Mosaic law, and that the Jews themselves should be freed from that yoke of bondage; these were discoveries totally new, and now revealed for the first time by the Spirit of God.
entries.2f7ab85cd12b1b8a3bd79050f44ac29854996bc6: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen50093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50094" type="x-p"/> That the Gentiles should be fellow heirs - This is the substance of that mystery which had been hidden from all ages, and which was now made known to the New Testament apostles and prophets, and more particularly to St. Paul. <div eID="gen50094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50095" type="x-p"/> His promise in Christ - That the promise made to Abraham extended to the Gentiles, the apostle has largely proved in his Epistle to the Romans; and that it was to be fulfilled to them by and through Christ, he proves there also; and particularly in his Epistle to the Galatians, see <reference osisRef="Gal.3.14">Gal 3:14</reference>. And that these blessings were to be announced in the preaching of the Gospel, and received on believing it, he every where declares, but more especially in this epistle.
entries.34c4fb708e71b4eab577f4c49c6648709ea37c75: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen50095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50096" type="x-p"/> Whereof I was made a minister - Διακονος· A deacon, a servant acting under and by the direction of the great Master, Jesus Christ; from whom, by an especial call and revelation, I received the apostolic gifts and office, and by την ενεργειαν της δυναμεως αυτου, the energy, the in-working of his power, this Gospel which I preached was made effectual to the salvation of vast multitudes of Jews and Gentiles.
entries.f4cd04488b38ec2135f090673e934e5c5407af92: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen50096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50097" type="x-p"/> Less than the least of all saints - Ελαχιστοτερῳ παντων ἁγιων. As the design of the apostle was to magnify the grace of Christ in the salvation of the world, he uses every precaution to prevent the eyes of the people from being turned to any thing but Christ crucified; and although he was obliged to speak of himself as the particular instrument which God had chosen to bring the Gentile world to the knowledge of the truth, yet he does it in such a manner as to show that the excellency of the power was of God, and not of him; and that, highly as he and his follow apostles were honored; they had the heavenly treasure in earthen vessels. To lay himself as low as possible, consistently with his being in the number of Divinely commissioned men, he calls himself less than the least; and is obliged to make a new word, by strangely forming a comparative degree, not from the positive, which would have been a regular grammatical procedure, but from the superlative. The adjective ελαχυς signifies little, ελασσων or ελαττων, less, and ελαχιστος, least. On this latter, which is the superlative of ελαχυς, little, St. Paul forms his comparative, ελαχιστοτερος, less than the least, a word of which it would be vain to attempt a better translation than that given in our own version. It most strongly marks the unparalleled humility of the apostle; and the amazing condescension of God, in favoring him, who had been before a persecutor and blasphemer, with the knowledge of this glorious scheme of human redemption, and the power to preach it so successfully among the Gentiles. <div eID="gen50097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50098" type="x-p"/> The unsearchable riches of Christ - The word ανεξιχνιαστος, from α, privative, and εξιχνιαζω, to trace out, from ιχνος, a step, is exceedingly well chosen here: it refers to the footsteps of God, the plans he had formed, the dispensations which he had published, and the innumerable providences which he had combined, to prepare, mature, and bring to full effect and view his gracious designs in the salvation of a ruined world, by the incarnation, passion, death, and resurrection of his Son. There were in these schemes and providences such riches - such an abundance, such a variety, as could not be comprehended even by the naturally vast, and, through the Divine inspiration, unparalleledly capacious mind of the apostle. <div eID="gen50098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50099" type="x-p"/> Yet he was to proclaim among the Gentiles these astonishing wonders and mysteries of grace; and as he proceeds in this great and glorious work, the Holy Spirit that dwelt in him opens to his mind more and more of those riches - leads him into those footsteps of the Almighty which could not be investigated by man nor angel, so that his preaching and epistles, taken all in their chronological order, will prove that his views brighten, and his discoveries become more numerous and more distinct in proportion as he advances. And had he lived, preached, and written to the present day, he had not exhausted the subject, nor fully declared to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ - the endless depths of wisdom and knowledge treasured up in him, and the infinity of saving acts and saving power displayed by him.
entries.11668b84c47d2c666e3895aae01dda20fa3d4a6c: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen50099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50100" type="x-p"/> And to make all men see - Και φωτισαι παντας· And to illuminate all; to give information both to Jews and Gentiles; to afford them a sufficiency of light, so that they might be able distinctly to discern the great objects exhibited in this Gospel. <div eID="gen50100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50101" type="x-p"/> What is the fellowship of the mystery - The word κοινωνια, which we properly translate fellowship, was used among the Greeks to signify their religious communities; here it may intimate the association of Jews and Gentiles in one Church or body, and their agreement in that glorious mystery which was now so fully opened relative to the salvation of both. But instead of κοινωνια, fellowship, οικονομια, dispensation or economy, is the reading of ABCDEFG, and more than fifty others; both the Syriac, Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Slavonian, Vulgate and Itala, with the chief of the Greek fathers. Some of the best printed editions of the Greek text have the same reading, and that in our common text has very little authority to support it. Dispensation or economy is far more congenial to the scope of the apostle's declaration in this place; he wished to show them the economy of that mystery of bringing Jews and Gentiles to salvation by faith in Christ Jesus, which God from the beginning of the world had kept hidden in his own infinite mind, and did not think proper to reveal even when he projected the creation of the world, which had respect to the economy of human redemption. And although the world was made by Jesus Christ, the great Redeemer, yet at that period this revelation of the power of God, the design of saving men, whose fall infinite wisdom had foreseen, was not then revealed. This reading Griesbach has received into the text. <div eID="gen50101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50102" type="x-p"/> Who created all things by Jesus Christ - Some very judicious critics are of opinion that this does not refer to the material creation; and that we should understand the whole as referring to the formation of all God's dispensations of grace, mercy, and truth, which have been planned, managed, and executed by Christ, from the foundation of the world to the present time. But the words δια Ιησου Χριστου, by Jesus Christ, are wanting in ABCD*FG, and several others; also in the Syriac, Arabic of Erpen, Coptic, Ethiopic, Vulgate, and Itala; as also in several of the fathers. Griesbach has thrown the words out of the text; and Professor White says, "certissime delenda," they are indisputably spurious. The text, therefore, should be read: which from the beginning of the world had been hidden in God who created all things. No inferiority of Christ can be argued from a clause of whose spuriousness there is the strongest evidence.
entries.cecb0d5ff8ad7dc72f8ea6931eb8229364fff87b: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen50102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50103" type="x-p"/> That now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places - Who are these principalities and powers? Some think evil angels are intended, because they are thus denominated, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.12">Eph 6:12</reference>. Others think good angels are meant; for as these heavenly beings are curious to investigate the wondrous economy of the Gospel, though they are not its immediate objects, see <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.12">1Pet 1:12</reference>, it is quite consistent with the goodness of God to give them that satisfaction which they require. And in this discovery of the Gospel plan of salvation, which reconciles things in heaven and things on earth - both men and angels, these pure spirits are greatly interested, and their praises to the Divine Being rendered much more abundant. Others imagine the Jewish rulers and rabbins are intended, particularly those of them who were converted to Christianity, and who had now learned from the preaching of the Gospel what, as Jews, they could never have known. I have had several opportunities of showing that this sort of phraseology is frequent among the Jews, and indeed not seldom used in the New Testament. Dr. Macknight, whose mode of arguing against this opinion is not well chosen, supposes that "the different orders of angels in heaven are intended, whose knowledge of God's dispensations must be as gradual as the dispensations themselves; consequently their knowledge of the manifold wisdom of God must have been greatly increased by the constitution of the Christian Church." Of this there can be no doubt, whether the terms in the text refer to them or not. <div eID="gen50103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50104" type="x-p"/> By the Church - That is, by the Christians and by the wonderful things done in the Church; and by the apostles, who were its pastors. <div eID="gen50104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50105" type="x-p"/> The manifold wisdom of God - Ἡ πολυποικιλος σοφια· That multifarious and greatly diversified wisdom of God; laying great and infinite plans, and accomplishing them by endless means, through the whole lapse of ages; making every occurrence subservient to the purposes of his infinite mercy and goodness. God's gracious design to save a lost world by Jesus Christ, could not be defeated by any cunning skill or malice of man or devils: whatever hinderances are thrown in the way, his wisdom and power can remove; and his infinite wisdom can never want ways or means to effect its gracious designs.
entries.6e8a8d1aded6661e336a292fdbe4d166068d9cb0: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen50105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50106" type="x-p"/> According to the eternal purpose - Κατα προθεσιν των αιωνων· According to the purpose concerning the periods. This seems to refer to the complete round of the Jewish system, and to that of the Gospel. I have often observed, that though the proper grammatical meaning of the word is ever-during or endless duration, yet it is often applied to those systems, periods, governments, etc., which have a complete duration, taking in the whole of them, from their commencement to their termination, leaving nothing of their duration unembraced. So, here, God purposed that the Jewish dispensation should commence at such a time, and terminate at such a time; that the Gospel dispensation should commence when the Jewish ended, and terminate only with life itself; and that the results of both should be endless. This is probably what is meant by the above phrase. <div eID="gen50106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50107" type="x-p"/> Which he purposed in Christ Jesus - Ἡν εποιησεν· Which he made or constituted in or for Christ Jesus. The manifestation of Christ, and the glory which should follow, were the grand objects which God kept in view in all his dispensations.
entries.3e4f151511505ecd8fe128946999c33c6bb6da10: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen50107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50108" type="x-p"/> In whom we have boldness - By whom we, Gentiles, have την παρῥησιαν, this liberty of speech; so that we may say any thing by prayer and supplication, and την προσαγωγην, this introduction, into the Divine presence by faith in Christ. It is only in his name we can pray to God, and it is only by him that we can come to God; none can give us an introduction but Christ Jesus, and it is only for his sake that God will either hear or save us. It is on the ground of such scriptures as these that we conclude all our prayers in the name, and for the sake, of Jesus Christ our Lord.
